newsitem.title: INDIA: India prepares last rites for air crash victims.
newsitem.headline: India prepares last rites for air crash victims.

text.p: India prepared a sombre ritual farewell on Thursday for victims of the world's worst mid-air collision, which killed some 350 people.
Experts said the cause of the crash could be determined inside two weeks following Wednesday's recovery of the black boxes from the wreckage of the two planes.
"We will perform the last rites of the victims who are too badly burned to be identified," Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim told reporters late on Wednesday.
The badly charred bodies will be cremated together.
Authorities have put together a list of passengers from manifests and from relatives of those aboard who came forward.
Indian authorities said they had handed over to relatives 70 identifiable bodies of some 254 which had been found. Sixty bodies were too badly mutilated to be identified.

There were no survivors among the 312 people aboard a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 that had just taken off from New Delhi on Tuesday evening or among the 37 people on a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter that was preparing to land.
Scores of distraught relatives thronged the general hospital at Charkhi Dadri, 80 kms (50 miles) west of Delhi in bordering Haryana state, hoping against hope to identify their loved ones.
The blazing wreckage of the two aircraft, which witnesses said plummeted to earth like "fireballs", fell 10 km (six miles) apart on the plain around Charkhi Dadri.
The wreckage of the Saudi plane was still smoking at dusk as searchers probed it for up to 60 more bodies they estimated could be recovered from under the debris.
The army was brought in to help clear the wreckage and search for bodies. It sent two helicopters and four medical teams, the Press Trust of India said.
Residents said they were sure the pilot of the jumbo averted an even worse disaster by steering his blazing aircraft away from their villages into nearby cotton and mustard fields.
Parveen Kumar of Charkhi Dadri town, which has a population of 50,000, told Reuters: "The plane turned into a fireball, and separated into three fireballs and fell into Dadri.
"I think the pilot deliberately went over the town and tried to land in the fields."
Ibrahim said 200 wooden coffins had been hastily prepared for the remains. Authorities arranged to embalm bodies destined for far-off places.

Aviation experts said it could take less than two weeks to ascertain the cause of the collision after searchers recovered the so-called "black boxes", or flight data and cockpit voice recorders, from the wreckage on Wednesday.
Speculation on the cause had ranged from inadequate equipment at New Delhi airport to pilots' misunderstanding of instructions from ground controllers.

Yogesh Chandra, the top civil servant at India's Civil Aviation Ministry, ruled out both. He said the transcript of the final conversations between the pilots and ground control showed both understood their instructions.
The transcript, which Chandra read to reporters, showed the pilots of both aircraft appeared to have understood instructions to maintain altitudes 1,000 feet (300 metres) apart.
The Saudi aircraft reported it was flying at 14,000 feet (4,270 metres) while the Kazakh plane said it was at 15,000 feet (4,575 metres).
Chandra said speculation that ageing equipment at Delhi airport might be to blame was "absolutely incorrect".
A new $92 million state-of-the-art air traffic control system being built by U.S. firm Raytheon for Bombay and Delhi airports would be operational by early next year, he added.

But pilots said the government had dragged its feet in installing the sophisticated radar equipment that would have permitted air traffic controllers in Delhi to establish the altitude of both aircraft as well as their direction.
Kazakhstan's state airline said the Il-76TD cargo plane had been in good technical condition.

Chandra refused comment on other possible causes raised by experts, including speculation the pilot of the KazAir plane could have misconverted the altitude instructions he was given in feet, the international norm, rather than metres.
The U.S. State Department said three Americans were aboard the Saudi Arabia Airlines plane. Deputy spokesman Glyn Davies said two of the Americans were passengers and one was a crew member.
Nepal's Foreign Ministry said there were 53 Nepalis on board, most of them headed for jobs as manual labourers, drivers and plumbers.
There were only three women, two American and one British, aboard.
The KazAir plane was carrying 25 businessmen who had chartered it to fly empty to Delhi, where they planned to buy $1.5 million worth of woollens for sale at home.
There were also two children and 10 crew on the plane, which broke in two. All 37 bodies were recovered.
